name: Microsoft PowerPoint
tagline: The default slide deck editor, bundled with Microsoft 365 and installed on roughly every corporate laptop on earth.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. PowerPoint is normally sold inside Microsoft 365 rather than standalone.

verdictSummary: You can absolutely one-shot a tool that turns text into slides and presents them fullscreen in a browser. What you cannot one-shot is .pptx, a decades-old XML format with thousands of edge cases that every reviewer, client, conference AV booth and university lecture hall expects to receive. The moment someone says 'send me the deck' you are back to a format you do not control, and partial exports look broken in ways that are embarrassing rather than charming. Add real-time co-authoring, comment threads, presenter view across two screens, and the template library your company's brand team already maintains, and the gap is not a weekend, it is a career. Build the markdown-to-slides thing because it is genuinely nicer for solo work, but keep PowerPoint installed.
coreLoopDIY: A local CLI that compiles a Markdown file into a self-contained HTML deck with speaker notes, keyboard navigation and PDF export.
requirements: A browser with headless PDF printing (Chromium via Playwright)
Willingness to write slides as text
whatYouLose: .pptx fidelity, both reading decks people send you and sending decks they can edit
Real-time co-authoring, comments, and version history that colleagues actually use
Designer and Copilot style suggestions that make an ugly deck passable in one click
Presenter view with timer, notes and next-slide preview across two displays
Mobile and tablet apps, plus the ability to present from a machine that is not yours
Animations, transitions, SmartArt, and the corporate template everyone else is already using
moatNotes: The format is the product. PowerPoint's real asset is that .pptx is the lingua franca of corporate communication, so every competitor spends most of its engineering budget on import fidelity rather than on being good.
whyPeopleStillPay: Almost nobody pays for PowerPoint on purpose. It arrives inside a Microsoft 365 subscription you already have for Outlook, Excel and Teams, which means the marginal cost of using it is zero and the marginal cost of not using it is explaining to a colleague why your deck opened with the fonts wrong. For solo thinking, a local Markdown deck tool is faster and calmer. For anything that gets reviewed, edited, projected or archived by other people, the file format wins and you open PowerPoint.
notes: A Markdown-to-HTML deck tool is a one-sitting build and genuinely pleasant for solo use. The moat is .pptx itself: a format every laptop, projector and reviewer on earth already agrees on, which no personal build gets to opt out of.
prompt:
Build a local command line tool called "deck" that compiles Markdown into a presentable HTML slide deck. Empty folder, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Node 20, TypeScript, run with tsx
- marked for Markdown, shiki for code highlighting
- Playwright (chromium) for PDF export only
- No framework, no bundler, no reveal.js dependency: write the deck runtime yourself in about 200 lines of vanilla JS

Input format: a single deck.md file. Slides are separated by lines containing exactly "---". Speaker notes are any block starting with "Notes:" at the end of a slide. Front matter at the top of the file (YAML-ish key: value lines between "---" fences) sets title, theme ("light" or "dark"), and accent color.

Commands:
- "deck build deck.md" writes dist/index.html as ONE self-contained file: inline CSS, inline JS, images base64-inlined from a local ./assets folder
- "deck watch deck.md" serves it on localhost:4321 and live-reloads over a plain EventSource on file change
- "deck pdf deck.md" prints dist/deck.pdf at 1280x720 via Playwright, one page per slide

Deck runtime requirements:
- Arrow keys, space, and swipe for next/previous; Home and End to jump
- "o" toggles a grid overview of all slides, click to jump
- "n" opens a separate notes window via window.open that stays in sync using BroadcastChannel, showing current notes, next slide text, and an elapsed timer
- Slide numbers, a thin progress bar, and the URL hash tracking the slide index so reloads land in place
- Code blocks highlighted at build time, not runtime
- Fits text by scaling a fixed 1280x720 stage with CSS transform so it looks identical everywhere

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: .pptx import or export, animations and transitions beyond a crossfade, multi-user editing, charts, themes beyond the two, any WYSIWYG editor.

Ship a README with a 10-line example deck.md, and an npm script "demo" that builds and opens it. No .env needed since there are no secrets.
